speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for two purposes today. The first is to make reference in a general way to the services of my friend the right hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. St. Laurent) and to say to him that without regard to party considerations I speak for the membership of this house when I re-express what I said on a previous occasion, namely that all of us deeply regret that his physical condition made it impossible for him to carry on and discharge the difficult and onerous responsibilities of leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
I speak as one who has known him for many years. On occasions such as this all of us who have been here for three or four parliaments, engaged in the service of our country, must be conscious of the advancing of the years. I knew him as president of the Canadian Bar Association; I knew him in his other capacities; when he came into the House of Commons in December, 1941, as minister of justice and attorney general, accepting the tremendous challenge of war as an incentive to entering into public life. I knew him as secretary of state for external affairs from September 4, 1946, and at the time he was chosen as leader of the Liberal party in August, 1948. I knew him at the beginning of his prime ministership on November 15, 1948, and I have also known him in the last few months in his capacity as leader of the opposition.
As was said on another occasion by one of my predecessors, Mr. King, when he was referring to Mr. Bennett, I am not here for the purpose of estimating the place to be given by posterity to the contribution he has made. I am here for the moment, however, to wipe aside those political controversies which separate us and to say this. We regret what has taken place. As I said before, whatever our political differences may be they have been exercised in the traditions of our citizenship and in the realization that each of us, from whatever part of the house
he may come, is making that contribution which according to his conscience represents the best for Canada.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
I say this as one who saw him in the courts as well as in the House of Commons; an outstanding lawyer and a representative recognized by the international councils, a prime minister who in his years of service made that kind of contribution which each of us, for ourselves, would be willing to have acknowledged at the conclusion of our public service.
It was said by Mr. King in a letter to Mr. Bennett at that time that the leadership of a great party taxes the health and strength and anyone who has held that position will recognize that statement as factually correct. But I can tell you one thing, I am back here better than ever.
Distinguished in his profession and an honoured parliamentarian, the right hon. gentleman has lived a rich and fruitful life. We are not here to evaluate his career. We are here simply to say to the right hon. gentleman that our hope is that the years ahead-and may they be many-will bring to him the happiness which comes from the realization that he has served his day and generation, because of no one could this be more truly said.
Next I wish to say to my hon. friend the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) that we on this side of the house extend to him our warmest congratulations on the achievement of his position as Leader of the Opposition, a position which is recognized under our system as an integral part of parliament. Indeed, in the work published by Lord Hailsham, as he now is, on parliament it is said:
Her Majesty's opposition is as definite and as formal a fact as Her Majesty's government.
I listened to the convention-

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
I followed the proceedings with that interest which one might expect. The hon. gentleman joined the Department of External Affairs in 1928. I met him first in 1934, I think it was, when he was secretary to the royal commission on price spreads set up by the then prime minister, Mr. Bennett. I saw him as an ambassador. I saw him at the United Nations

Leader of the Opposition in 1945; and since 1948 he has been a member of this chamber, until only recently as secretary of state for external affairs.
May I say this, that his service has been distinguished. His opportunities for service are greatly increased as a result of the responsibility which has now come to him. Hon. members would not expect me to say more than this: that I wish him health and happiness; I wish for him the opportunity to make that contribution which he is now in a position to make in the days ahead. I congratulate him, and extend to him my best wishes in that regard.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I too rise for the twofold purpose the Prime Minister had in mind when he rose to speak a few moments ago: first, to pay tribute to the right hon. gentleman who led the government for so long and the opposition until today. I hope he will have health and strength to remain with us and to give the parliament of Canada the advice he can give for a good many years yet.
The right hon. gentleman came here, I remember, in 1942 at a time of very great difficulty during the war, and gave freely of himself, having relinquished the practice of a profession in which he not only shone but, indeed, gloried. That was a great sacrifice on his part, and I think the country appreciated it, just as the country appreciates the services he has rendered to this nation as minister of justice, as minister of external affairs and as prime minister. And I am quite sure the right hon. gentleman knows that, whatever the fortunes of his party on June 10 of last year, that was no reflection upon the former prime minister himself.
We join the Prime Minister in expressing our regret that he has felt it necessary to lay down the reins of the leadership in which he was so distinguished and in wishing him well in the future.
I want to join the Prime Minister, too, in congratulating the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson). I have known him now for a number of years and have been closely associated with him from time to time at international conferences. I have the highest regard and the greatest respect for him, and his only misfortune is that he is associated with the Liberal party. I could wish otherwise, because I have sometimes found my own mind running along the same channels as the hon. gentleman's mind in international affairs at least.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext: You are in the wrong party, really.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
I have always thought I was in the right party, and as long as I think so I shall remain in what I consider to be the right party.
I join, too, in wishing him health and strength so that he may carry on in the high office to which he has been called by the party; now, of course, occupying as he does -what shall I say-the third highest position in this House of Commons; first the Speaker, then the Prime Minister and then the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. In that capacity we wish him well, and it is a capacity I hope he will fill in this house for at least some time.
I am not going to express a further opinion on this occasion; but, Mr. Speaker, we wish to join the Prime Minister in what he has said regarding the hon. member for Quebec East and the hon. member for Algoma East. We hope both will find happiness in the days to come.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Prime Minister has expressed sentiments which we in this group sincerely feel toward the retiring leader of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Quebec East. On this occasion when he is relinquishing his duties as leader of the official opposition and of his party we want him to know that we have toward him nothing but good will, and we wish him many years of happy and abundant living. We hope he will be around the House of Commons for quite a while to come, because I am sure that his experience and wise counsel will be very much needed and freely called upon.
I want also to join with those who have preceded me in expressing sincere congratulations to the new leader of the official opposition. It is not often that a man wins in so short a space of time two such great honours as those won by the hon. member for Algoma East. Of the two, of course, the one carrying with it the greatest responsibility and demanding the hardest and most unremitting effort is that of the leadership of his party and of the official opposition in this house.
I am sure the new Leader of the Opposition knows he will be expected to restore Liberal fortunes, to use his own word, "soon". He will be expected to keep his promises and all the promises made by his party. The people of Canada will remind him with embarrassing frequency, I am sure, of those parts of his nomination speech in which he said, "Liberalism must everlastingly insist on the freedom of the individual against the state".

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
And again those words, "the price of security and fair share of income to which the farmer is entitled". Canadians will keep throwing his words back in his face until every jot and tittle of their implications have been fulfilled.
The leadership of any one of the Canadian political parties is a tough job. Especially is this so of the Liberal party at this time, a party which has had many years in office and comparatively few years in opposition. On behalf of the group I am leading in this house I want to extend to the new Leader of the Opposition our sincerest good wishes, and to assure him we do hope that in the years ahead his health and strength will be always somewhat greater than the demands that will be made upon them by his heavy duties in this house and as the leader of his party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Quebec East):
maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been many deeply moving occasions in the course of the years I have been a member of this house, but none more than that of this afternoon. All I can say is to express to the Prime Minister, to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and to the hon. member for Peace River my very deep thanks for the kind words they have said about me on this occasion. Not only will those words be recorded in the reports of the debates of this house, but they will always be engraved in my memory, and will give me an additional reason to try and achieve everything implied in the good wishes that have been expressed on my behalf this afternoon.
I am not taking leave of the house at this moment. I enjoy the fellowship which it has been my privilege to enjoy over the years, and I wish to echo the words of the Prime Minister. Though we do differ on many occasions in this house, we do not differ upon his assumption that each one is endeavouring to do that which he thinks is in the best interests of his fellow citizens, and that is our only justification for occupying places in this house. Oh, of course we do all make mistakes, but I hope the mistakes can always be overlooked, if not forgotten, as generously as they have been this afternoon in the remarks of the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Peace River.
That being so, I can say to those who are much younger than I that there is a great satisfaction, in spite of our human frailties, in the feeling that as members of this house we have the opportunity to be of some service to this great country.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO OLD, WELCOME TO NEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is for me an occasion on which it is impossible not to be moved
Leader of the Opposition to the point where it is difficult for me to speak. I thank the Prime Minister for his friendly and gracious observations. Perhaps I might add that we were both away from the house last week, and I am delighted to see him back better than ever.
May I also thank my old friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar for what he was good enough to say, and my friend the hon. member for Peace River, though I confess that he did make me even more conscious of the responsibilities and difficulties of my new position than I was even before.
I do appreciate more than I can say the friendly reception I have been given by the house, at least on this occasion. On my transition with almost bewildering rapidity from my commons seat of Saturday to that of today, I had no opportunity to enjoy and profit by that period of post-convention rest and reflection which my predecessors were,
I understand, able to enjoy. It was not, of course, a case of out of the frying pan into the fire, but it certainly was one of out of the convention and into the commons, which is a good place to be.
I have known the Prime Minister and the other two hon. members of the house who were good enough to speak for some years now. Their words today, Mr. Speaker, are one more evidence of the friendly feelings I have always encountered from members on both sides of the house since I first took my seat here nearly 10 years ago; feelings which are able to transcend party differences and which do reflect not only personal regard, I hope, but reflect the fact that we are all working together here as believers in responsible and stable democratic government, and that in our different ways we are all doing our best to serve the public interest.
Perhaps there is no more dramatic indication of the difference between our system of free parliamentary government and that of communist totalitarian rule than the position I now hold as leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. I have, for instance, this afternoon been the recipient of the good wishes of those to whose removal from office I am dedicated. I am even now the recipient of a salary from the crown to encourage me in that laudable and practicable endeavour. If as Leader of the Opposition-and this is another happy contrast with communist traditions and practices-I lose my head, it will only be in a political and temperamental, not in a physical sense.
On January 26, 1949, when the right hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. St. Laurent)- and it is difficult for me to refer to him in that capacity-spoke about the new leader of

Canadian National Railways the opposition, Mr. Drew, who was being introduced in the house that day, he said:
The position of Leader of the Opposition is a very high and honourable one. It requires a rare combination of qualities, a knowledge of public affairs and the ability to criticize firmly and boldly on proper occasions, but also the ability to discriminate between proper occasions and times when mere wordy outpourings would be anything but constructive.
I shall do my best to live up to that high conception of my office. I shall also, as leader of my party, try to be worthy in some degree at least of the example set by my predecessor. Canadian public life has had no greater gentleman or worthier or more respected servant than he was and is.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I shall also try my very best to emulate my right hon. friend the Prime Minister in at least one respect as Leader of the Opposition; namely, to stay in this position for as short a time as he was successful in doing.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPLEMENTARY WINTER WORK PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to make an announcement which I feel sure will be very well received by all members of the house. Before making it I should like to say that I received representations on this matter from all the members from Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy), and several other hon. members who have spoken to me about this matter. This is a press release issued today by the management of Canadian National Railways.
Following a meeting of senior operating officials from all regions in Canada, Canadian National Railways announced today that a supplementary winter work program would go into effect immediately in an effort to avoid any further reduction of employment on its Canadian lines during the winter months. This decision was made in response to an appeal by the federal government,

which is being directed to industry generally, including all railways, to the effect that they take special responsibility for their own work forces during this winter period when unemployment normally develops.
The management of Canadian National Railways deems it in the national interest to respond to the request of the government by embarking on work programs aimed at keeping the regular labour force employed on work that would not normally be undertaken in winter months, or which would be deferred until traffic earnings justify it.
While this may add somewhat to the cost of such work, and as well make it more difficult to reverse the deficit which appeared in the 1957 operations of Canadian National Railways, nevertheless the circumstances are such that management believes it is prudent to avoid, as far as possible, the disorganizing effects of massive short-term unemployment during this winter season. Consequently all supervisory officers have been directed to explore ways and means of organizing supplementary work programs in local areas throughout Canada, with the objective that Canadian National Railways will not contribute to further winter unemployment.
The supplementary work programs will not mean new hirings, but are of course being designed to keep the existing labour force employed. These programs will require the interested co-operation of the various labour groups, and must be sufficiently flexible to meet the varying needs of local areas. Consequently they will be under the direction of local and regional supervisory officers.
The supplementary work programs now being put into effect will be in addition to the accelerated works programs on capital account which were announced by Canadian National Railways on December 20 to provide employment for some 600 men on projects estimated to cost $3,500,000. This was made possible through advance approval by the government of a portion of the 1958 budget of the railway.
No estimate can be made of the cost of the new programs now being organized, but the nature of the work will, for the most part, be a charge to operating expense.

Mr. Speaker, the house will be pleased to know that the statement I made in the house on January 14 on the campground-picnic area program has been received very favourably by the provinces. At that time I mentioned that five provinces officially and one unofficially had been heard from. Since then I have received official advice from Ontario and have heard from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Manitoba.
The situation is that at the present time nine provinces have joined in this program most enthusiastically. Therefore on the forest access road program and the campground-picnic site program the expectations of the government have been far exceeded in the co-operation and enthusiastic response by the provinces. It means that the amounts we have mentioned will probably be slightly exceeded, but I think there is a deeper significance than that to this announcement.
We originally embarked on this program to provide seasonal employment, but now not only will we be providing pleasant places for travellers to stop and improve the hospitality of our highways not only for Canadians but for visitors coming to Canada but I think we will be providing safety for motorists. If this program which has been announced can improve safety on any roads in Canada I think we can all appreciate the effect and significance of the work we have done at this time.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised a question as to whether Canadian Pacific Airlines could be required to carry out its repair and overhaul work in Canada. It is my understanding that in fact C.P.A. does carry out its major overhaul and maintenance work at its base in Vancouver, where it has already invested many thousands of dollars in extensive facilities for this purpose, and that maintenance work is done outside the country only in accordance with the requirements of operational expediency.
In any case, examination of my authority under the Aeronautics Act has led me to the conclusion that it would scarcely be a proper exercise of my authority thereunder to issue orders or to place restrictions on Canadian air lines in the manner suggested by my hon. friend.
May I also remind him that C.P.A., like T.C.A., operates to many foreign countries and must comply with the legal requirements of those foreign countries too in the matter of local operation and organization.

May I explain to him that the phrase "subject to governmental approval" meant that the proposed new fares had not yet received the approval of the air transport board, which exercises jurisdiction over all air line fares but that in this respect C.P.A. is not proposing anything materially different from T.C.A. or any other international air line, since international fares in this category are set on a uniform basis as a result of discussions among the members of the international air transport association, including both C.P.A. and T.C.A., and then submitted for approval of the respective international aeronautical authorities concerned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion, apart from that happy one of a few moments ago, on which I have had to speak in my new capacity; and I am very conscious of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that I do so in circumstances and at a time not exactly of my own choosing. I am also very conscious of the fact that I am speaking at a serious time in the history of our country, and indeed in the history of the world; that domestic and international problems are such that they demand action characterized on the part of every single person concerned-and that includes all of us-by responsibility and a clear recognition of the national interest.
It is my duty, of course, as leader of the official opposition, guided I hope always by the considerations which I have just mentioned, to point out whenever it is required and to drive home as vigorously as I can, the inadequacy of government measures, the sins of omission and commission of the government in the handling of current problems which, as I have indicated, are serious and difficult, problems which face us now to an extent and in a manner not even contemplated last June.
I think it will be agreed, Mr. Speaker, that proposals for vigorous and effective domestic action are certainly required at this moment, in view of the trade and unemployment situation in this country. If we on this side of

There are threats to our exports to the United States of base metals and fish. These are not to be taken lightly having regard to the effect that they will have on our trade. I can assure the government that we on this side will back to the limit any efforts which they make-and they are making efforts-with the government of the United States to get that former restriction removed and to prevent the latter. Then finally may I say this. It is clear now that our total trade has ceased to expand and that our export markets are threatened, that proposals for freer trade have been rebuffed and that some encouragement-and I think it is fair to say this-has been given to United States protectionist forces which it is devoutly to be hoped by us all will be kept in check in Washington.
Part of the decline in trade and business is I think owing to the decline in actual private investment and even more to the serious decline in investment intention, and we are in the midst of what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has referred to as an economic pause. Of course, part of this decline in investment results from world conditions. There is no doubt about that fact, and that is something over which no national government can exercise anything but a measure of control and influence. This declining investment is, of course, one of the causes of mounting unemployment. Hence I believe there is real need to restore the climate of confidence, to reassure potential investors, to remove fear of the future and meanwhile to step up public investment in Canada in order to take in some of the slack in employment in this country. Something has been done by the government in this field but I suggest that not enough has been done. There have been housing loans and they have been welcome, but not very extensive measures with regard to national parks, forests and picnic grounds which, I think in view of the fact that the maximum amount which they are likely to give is between $3,000 and $4,000, are hardly likely to be an adequate contribution to the needs of employment in this field. What is needed is bold and imaginative action by the government while a favourable climate is being restored. The fear of unemployment is our greatest fear in this country today next to war itself. To remove that fear I suggest that we should get back on the Liberal road to expanding trade, expanding investment and expanding employment.
Then there is the agricultural question and the problems of farmers and primary producers. As we know, farmers are and have been for some time caught in the price squeeze. We also know that they were promised quick and welcome relief by my hon. friends opposite. What have they been offered? They have been offered one bill, Mr. Speaker, which called forth such violent protests from agricultural organizations that it had to be rewritten and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) had to get the unanimous consent of the house to substitute a new bill with which the farmers are not yet satisfied. Indeed, many believe that the new bill is not as good as the Liberal price support legislation of 1944. We take the view Mr. Speaker, that what is now required is not so much new legislation as new policy. I would refer to the resolution on agriculture adopted by the National Liberal convention as an indication of what that policy should be. Loggers are already depressed by the drastic decline in the pulpwood market and the whole fishing industry is apprehensive about these United States tariff changes which they have good cause to fear. The miners are worried by the same threat from south of the border.

speechtext: -and so worded as to assure that there is no possibility of this government being defeated.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How do you know?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I would suggest to my hon. friends opposite that it is not so very long ago in the pipe-line debate when they sang a hymn-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Who debased the flag?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
*-and I would suggest they recall that to mind now. It is so worded -and the truth hurts-that it is understood even by those who cannot understand, such
as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). Listen to the wording:
And in view of the desirability, at this time, of having a government pledged to implement Liberal policies;
His Excellency's advisers should, in the opinion of this house, submit their resignation forthwith.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) gave the answer today. There was a byelection in Lanark which gave the answer; there was a by-election in Wellington South which gave the answer. The only reason that this amendment is worded as it is is that my hon. friends opposite quake when they think of what will happen if an election comes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Call it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I do not mind, but there was a day when noises such as that passed for argument but no longer. They worded the amendment as it is because they realize that there is no party in this house, other than themselves, that wants to see a government pledged to implement the Liberal policies forthwith. Oh, Mr. Speaker, I heard my hon. friend say in courageous tones, "Stand up or talk up". Today he talked up but they are afraid to stand up. He produced an amendment. Ordinarily the other parties are provided with a copy of the amendment at least when the speech begins. But let us take the various things, and I am not going to deal with them in detail.
Canada's total trade has ceased to expand.
That is not true.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Canada's trade has
expanded in the year 1957, over the previous year-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: For the first six months.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will you please have at least some degree of order.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I do not think either side of the house is entitled to call the other side names. There has been a great deal of enthusiasm displayed but I would ask hon. members to hear the speaker in silence so that he does not have to ask for order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I mentioned a moment ago that Canada's total trade is expanding and has expanded. The amendment goes on to say:
Export markets have been threatened.
3522	HOUSE OF

I shall deal with that in a moment, but I shall leave the expansion of our arguments to my hon. friends, the ministers in question. The amendment says:
That investment has been discouraged and unemployment has risen drastically.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: True.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I intend to show when that started and that my hon. friends opposite were warned but did nothing.
My hon. friend said there are problems today that were not even contemplated last June. I intend to establish as clearly as the printed word will make possible that during the months of March, April, May until June 10, my hon. friends concealed from the Canadian people the facts. They know that. Oh, what crocodile tears are shed over the farmers. The amendment says:
That farmers and other primary producers have been disillusioned and discouraged.
My hon. friend says, look at our policies, look at what we have done. Well, I do not know to which policies he refers because I read this.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: You have not any.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
There was the greatest loss of resolutions. Somewhere between the brass and the grass the resolutions got lost. I will have to put my glasses on in order to see this fine print.
Scores of policy resolutions presented from the floor of the national Liberal convention this week vanished without trace.
Do you think it was the grass that took them away? I ask you, Mr. Speaker.
Proposals sponsored by provincial delegates or other groups were shunted to the 150-member resolutions committee for consideration.
They were lost, Mr. Speaker, because of the fact that the same group who have not realized yet that they were defeated on June 10 are still directing affairs.
My hon. friend says, "Look at the agricultural resolutions". I read them with interest, for almost every one of them-I can almost say every one of them-was voted against by the persons who today say they are good for the country. When they had the power, what did they do about a system of support prices except the sham and the caricature that was on the statute books? What did they do?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Brought them in.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What did they do to assure the farmers a fair share of the national income? Whenever we moved a resolution to that effect they voted against it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What did you do on the C.C.F. resolution? You ducked to cover.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
What did they do to encourage the production of marketable farm products? Listen to this:
Making available to grain producers not covered by the wheat board act a program of cash advances.
Before June last they said it could not be done. They said we would not be able to put cash advances on the statute books. They said cash advances were no good, they were no better than their loan plan. This afternoon my hon. friend used the expression, "Merely a loan, after all, without interest". They said it could not be done. They grudgingly supported it in the house. Now they come back, Mr. Speaker. Repentance is always worth while, even though it is in the face of impending disaster. I read on:
Assistance in setting up plans of accident compensation to the farmer.
What did they do in that regard in 22 years? They said it could not be done. I read on:
A policy of soil and water conservation.
Whenever a motion to that effect was made in the house they opposed it. I continue:
Extension of the principles of the P.F.R.A. to the whole of Canada.
Whenever that question was raised the answer given was that it was inappropriate. I go on.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Tell us about the South Saskatchewan dam while you are on that subject.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Here is another good one:
Provision for accelerated depreciation on buildings constructed on farms for the storage of farm products.
Whenever we brought that matter before the house the party then in power, now sitting in opposition today, voted against it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Why didn't you do it in the
last seven months?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I continue:
Establishment of a joint federal-provincial agricultural advisory board which would investigate farm problems and recommend public policies.
They were 22 years in power but they never learned about it, Mr. Speaker, until the grass was permitted to look at the brass at the convention. This is just one of the examples, and I have taken it because it was referred to by my hon. friend. It is an example of a policy created because of their position of fear, realizing that they have not done the things that they ought to have done. They think the people of Canada will forget that these things that they now advocate on every opportunity that came to them they

Suggested Resignation of Government
voted against. Then, they say that relations with provincial governments have deteriorated. How did they deteriorate? They said one time that the provincial governments would get less if this party came into power. I said no.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: They are getting nothing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Words, words, words.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What is Nova Scotia getting?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: My hon. friends say they are getting nothing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Well, let him say that in the maritime provinces.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: They have not got anything yet.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We are giving every consideration to this matter, not to reduce amounts but to assure a reasonable opportunity for the provinces to carry into effect those policies which we have advocated, those things that come peculiarly within provincial and municipal jurisdiction, and our intention is do that thing at the earliest opportunity.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: When is that?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: "That the budget is no longer in balance"-that statement is simply a statement unsupported by facts-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Because there is no budget.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: -and simply generated in enthusiasm. "Revenues are declining, expenditures are rising, day to day expedients have been substituted for firm and steady administration." I would be less than frank if I did not tell you Mr. Speaker, that it is difficult to carry on a government with minority representation when my hon. friends of the official opposition criticize in the house, orate against what is introduced and then when the vote comes vote with us. It has been a sorry spectacle.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The once great Liberal party.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
"And in view of the desirability at this time of having a government pledged to implement Liberal policies" Mr. Speaker, they are pretty frightened that they might have to undergo an election. Did you hear the explanations? They want the people to have more time to learn of what is happening in parliament. If the people do not know as a result of the conduct of the present opposition during the past three or four months, then that opposition has not been doing its duty.
The hon. gentleman says, "we do not want to vote out the government; all we want to
do is turn back the clock so that the people of Canada shall not have the right to say at this time who shall be the government in the next few years."
Mr. Speaker, I could not have believed that a great party would produce such a pusillanimous collection of criticism. If they believe what they say; if, as my hon. friend contended in stentorian tones, the majority of the people voted for them-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: He did not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
-what are they so
frightened about? They boast about that but that was not so in 1953. They had an overwhelming majority in the house even though they represented a minority of the Canadian people. No, Mr. Speaker, as far as this amendment is concerned it is simply designed to pretend, to pretend to stand up as my hon. friend spoke up. Have they any idea that any party in this house would want to see them beck in power?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: plague on both your houses.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak of this amendment in crushing terms, but there is no other expression that can be applied to it than this. It is the resignation from responsibility of a great party. It is a program designed in a spirit of resignation while at the same time pretending to the Canadian people that it is designed to be courageous. If my hon. friend were to tell you what is in his heart of hearts he would frankly admit that when this was drawn it represented a compromise between the fearless who have no regard to realities, who would like to have an election now, and the other more thoughtful ones who, having had the experience of sitting on the treasury benches, are afraid to challenge but want to appear valiant. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the resignation amendment of a party saturated with fear of what the electorate will do to it.
I was particularly impressed with my hon. friend when he said that the problems that face Canada today were not even contemplated last June. I shall be dealing with that in a moment in a record that cannot be denied. However, I think I should first make some reference to what this party has done under difficult circumstances. We have reduced taxes-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How much?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: -in order to stimulate-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How much?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: They say how much, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
You promised $500 million.
3524	HOUSE OF
Suggested Resignation of Government

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: When we have the authority we shall do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Why don't you find out whether or not you have it?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We made $300 million available to swell the flow of funds into house building. The results have been most gratifying. Housing starts in municipalities having a population of 5,000 and over ranged between 70,000 and 80,000, seasonally adjusted, during the past summer. They rose by 92.4 per cent in October and the November figure was 217,000, the largest ever recorded for that month.
Across the way, Mr. Speaker, sit the purveyors of gloom who would endeavour, for political purposes, to panic the Canadian people at this time. One of the first things we did was to bring about amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to extend the period so as to put many millions of dollars into the hands of those who are unemployed who will need it this winter and spring and who have needed it in years past. We increased pensions and veterans allowances. We are endeavouring to bring in farm supports that will assure the Canadian farmer for the first time of that which over the years Canadian farm organizations have desired, namely a fair share of the national income.
We have also made provision that spending on public works shall be accelerated in order to stimulate employment. We brought into effect cash advances on farm-stored wheat. Let me say this. These prophesiers of doom said for political purposes that we would not be able to export wheat-we found difficulties; they had lost the markets-but in the month of November we exported more wheat than in November the year before.
In addition to that legislation on behalf of the maritimes in regard to the development of power we intend to provide as well special assistance to those provinces by the sea that are in need. We have done that in the face of an opposition-and I am speaking at the moment of the official opposition-which attacked everything, endeavoured to thwart by argument and then, with that same high courage that characterized this amendment today they spoke up but when the vote came they voted contrary to what they said.
My hon. friend says, "We have produced a wonderful platform". "Nothing has been done for the maritimes", said that pundit the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). What did Premier Matheson of


Prince Edward Island say? He arrived in Ottawa on January 13. On arrival in Ottawa he said this:
His party will seek a better deal for the maritimes from the Federal Liberal party.
What about the other deals they got from the Liberal party? Then he used these words, and you cannot call him a biased witness:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker is giving it to us so why can't the Liberals?
That is what the Liberal premier said. He said, "That is why the Liberals were defeated last June." From the mouths of those who know, Mr. Speaker, shall be quoted the truth. My friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, "What have they done for the maritimes?"

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend, not understanding, cannot appreciate what Mr. Matheson said. He said:
That is why the Liberals were defeated last June. They did not give the maritimes half a deal.
I thought that should be on the record, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will permit a question since he has drawn me into the discussion. The question I should like to ask the Prime Minister is this. Why then did the government refuse the perfectly proper request of the premier of Newfoundland? That is all we discussed on this side of the house.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Why did my hon. friend, when he was in office, not do somehting for Newfoundland which saw him an orphan, without a seat, and took him in?
I do not want to cover the record thoroughly today-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I can understand that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
If that is one thing the hon. member can understand, it is the first thing he has understood since I have been in this house.
The question is asked as to what we did in the opposition in the months preceding the election. We warned the government that it was following a reckless course. We told them it was going contrary to the views of economists. As far as trade is concerned, we told them that it was diminishing because it was being lost. We told them that it was not acting in the first interests of Canada. After all, Canadian interests should come first.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend says "no". That apparently is the policy of the opposition.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
He did not say "No", he said "oh, oh".

Suggested Resignation of Government

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We told them that the situation was very serious. We told them that to too great an extent they were putting the Canadian trade eggs into one basket. We told them that if the day ever came in the United States when anything in the nature of a recession or a pause should take place the consequences would be detrimental to Canada, for if there is one thing United States governments do when their people suffer, it is to act on behalf of their people.
I am not going to rehash what happened in 1921 when Canadian agricultural products were closed out of the United States nor what happened in June of 1930 when similar action was taken on the part of the United States. The same situation has been prevalent during the last few years. Look at the record of our exports to the United States in farm products. When any farm product in any way interferes with the United States people, the administration of the United States acts. We pointed out in the spring of this year that deflationary influences would be dominant during 1957. We warned that both labour and materials were moving into excess supply right down the line. What did they do, these paragons of political perfection in reverse? What did they do then? They know what to do today but what did they do then?
They based their government policy on the consideration that there was to be no end to the boom. They did not realize the situation or if they did so they concealed the facts from the Canadian people; and I think the latter is the better explanation as will be revealed as I quote from certain government documents. They continued their policy of a tremendous surplus on budget. They refused to consider the easing of tight money. They followed a course which we warned would lead to unemployment and to the destruction of trade.
My hon. friend says, "We did not know about these things; they did not exist in June last". May I point out that over and over again the former government were warned in these words, "Unemployment is increasing". Does my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition say that he was not told that? Silence gives the answer, Mr. Speaker. They were told that unemployment was going to mount.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That speech was made by Mr. Bennett in 1930.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I am going to read from a government document. In the first five months of 1957 unemployment was consistently higher than it was in the corresponding months in 1956.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister permit a question?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Is he not aware that in the month of March the work force in Canada was at its highest peak in history?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not aware of the fact that the same situation prevailed all fall?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: With 800,000 unemployed?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: In March of 1957 those without jobs and seeking work were 6 per cent of the civilian working force compared to 5.3 per cent in 1956 and almost identical with the 6.1 per cent in 1951. The only time it was ever worse was during the recognized recession of 1955.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: You speak like another Tory government.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is about as intelligent an interruption as has ever come from that source in the past. It was only worse, with 7.4 per cent, in the recession winter of 1955 when those who today say they should be over here were in power. Early in 1957 unemployment was at practically the same percentage as it was in the difficult winter of 1954 and not far below the levels prevailing in the worst post-war winter of 1955. What did they do then?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What did you say then?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What did the Liberals do; that is what I am asking. They simply said the condition did not exist. They continued their policy of tight money, failing to put into circulation the necessary money in order to help the house building industry in this country and thereby, in a measure, restore the lumber industry.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: House building was at a record of 137,000 units in that year.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not have his records up to date and I would ask him to look at them again. In spite of this evidence and in spite of these warnings, those who today say they would like to be over here-they do not realize there was a June 10 -said their actions at that time had been taken to restrain a non-existent boom. They did not realize the bloom was coming oft the boom. They did not realize that deflationary forces had replaced inflationary ones as the dominating influence working in the economy of Canada.
3526	HOUSE OF
Suggested Resignation of Government
I said a moment ago that I was going to quote from the record. This record was in the possession of each and every minister in the former government. They knew the situation in March last unless they were like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who by his own admission a moment ago has never read it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Never read what?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
They went ahead with the policy which could not but accelerate the forces that were bringing about a deflationary condition in Canada. I am going to now read from this document in order to answer my hon. friend who the other night said "In June there was no problem of unemployment; our trade was at the highest level; we had an expanding economy."
Today one looks back and realizes that these men who were in power did not do that of which my hon. friend spoke in such colourful terms the other night. He said we must not conceal facts, but I put it to the hon. members opposite-every one of them in the official opposition-that they hid the facts; they concealed the record; they did not let the Canadian people know what was taking place.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Like your budget?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: You budgeted for a surplus when the economic situation clearly called for a balanced budget. You failed to reduce taxation. You failed to put money in circulation. What did you do to the old people of this country?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
You turned a deaf ear to the warnings of rising interest rates, strangling business activity and raising the costs. You turned a deaf ear to the requests to assist industries in difficulty to meet legitimate regional demands.
The result was a drastic reduction in house building and the lumber industry was placed in a position where it had lost those markets abroad which it previously enjoyed and at the same time was losing its market in Canada. You secured the advice of the economists in your own departments and were advised as to what the situation was in March 1957. This record was given to each and every one of you-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the right hon. gentleman what he is reading from?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I thought the hon. gentleman knew of it before, but I am reading from the report "Canadian Economic Outlook" prepared by the economic branch of


the Department of Trade and Commerce delivered in March 1957 at a time when my hon. friends opposite were telling the Canadian people how well things were going and were refusing to act. I am now going to read from what the report recommended. It says some of the symptoms that typically are found in the latter stages of a cyclical expansion have begun to appear and such indications have tended to become more apparent since the turn of the year; more conficting tendencies in construction and manufacturing have entered and increases in unemployment in Canada since October have been much more than seasonal.
Regarding Canadian industry it says-at a time when Canadian industry needed help- that the competitive position of Canadian manufacturing has deteriorated markedly since 1950 with respect to both the United States and other major manufacturing countries. It says the most rapid period of deterioration was from 1950 to 1952 but a moderate further deterioration has taken place in the last 18 months.
After that warning what did they do? We have heard a great deal, of course, about the United States and about the money that has been invested by United States citizens. I have not seen any particular reduction in that excepting in the same proportion in which Americans are investing in their own industry today. In other words, there has been a very marked fall-away with which I intend to deal if I have time. In the United States in the period since January last this has been evident in the stock markets and in production; surpluses have been piling up and unemployment there has risen to the highest point in many years. Surely my hon. friends opposite, who tied Canada's economy to such a degree to that of the United States both with respect to our import and export business, must have expected that if an economic deterioration took place in the United States it would have its effect in Canada.
The report says later on that postwar developments are such that the inter-relations between Canadian and United States economies are even closer than previously and that exports to the United States have become a large part of total Canadian exports and have been larger in relation to total domestic output in recent years than in the 1920's. It also says that Canada had become more dependent on the United States as a source of imports of both merchandise and capital, and that underlying physical and psychological forces are both likely to ensure more similar rather than less similar developments for the two economies in the years immediately ahead.

Do my hon. friends say that this government is responsible for the fact that in the United States during the last eight or nine months there has been such a rapid deterioration in economic wellbeing as compared with the boom days? Do my hon. friends suggest, even though they thrive in endeavouring to fill the Canadian people with panic for political purposes-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Do they suggest that the influence of the United States with its vast economy does not affect us here in Canada? Instead of being fair, instead of being reasonable, they who for 22 years provided the climate for this circumstance now have the effrontery to say to us that because conditions here-in common with what is happening the United States-are not as they were at the height of the boom, therefore this government is responsible.
They had a warning. They could not deny that they had this warning, clear and definite. What about this?
During 1956 the Canadian economy has begun to show some of the symptoms usually found only in the last stages of a cyclical expansion.
Did they tell us that? They were warned what would happen.
Increases in demand in exports and investment have begun to moderate and this is likely to become more apparent during the coming years.
That was in March, 1957; the economists whom they chose to study these matters forecast that later on in the year investment from the United States would begin to moderate.
It has become apparent that after increasing more rapidly than in the United States in the first half of the year the rate of increase definitely slackened and was slower than in the United States since July. These tendencies, tentative and incomplete as they admittedly are, suggest that more caution on the outlook is appropriate at this time.

I spoke on this subject at Dartmouth University and I was amazed by the fact that from all over the United States letters were sent to me saying that Canada had a legitimate grievance; that we were placed in a position where the United States exploited our raw materials and our semimanufactured goods while at the same time closing out, generally speaking, our agricultural exports to the United States.
I propose to read part of a short summary of an article which appeared in Barrons magazine on December 30, 1957. It is entitled: "United States must End Economic Warfare Against Canada." It reads:
The United States in short has showered down good will upon the four corners of the earth. Closer to home, however-virtually in its own backyard- it has chosen to behave in contrary fashion. In particular, in terms of trade policy this country long has acted badly toward the Dominion of Canada. Heedless of damage to the wheat growers of Manitoba, the administration has sanctioned the dumping of domestic surpluses on the world market. Similarly, it has confronted the Canadian mining industries with the threat of higher tariffs on non-ferrous metals. Finally, over the strenuous protests of Ottawa-and in violation of its own commitments-Washington last week decreed the extension of "voluntary" quotas on foreign oil, including Canadian crude, to the west coast. Such moves undoubtedly have pleased, if not appeased, various special interests at home.
The article goes on:
Canada has deserved well of this country. Instead somehow it has become a favourite whipping boy of various United States agencies and interests. Several years ago, for example, customs authorities reclassified Canadian ping pong balls as ammunition-they can be used in pop guns-thereby raising the duty on them nine-fold.
Then the article goes on to discuss the picture generally. Anyone may read this article who wishes to do so. It finally ends with the warning that such conditions cannot be allowed to continue.

I am not going to add to anything that I said at the beginning, but I must say that when the C.C.F. come along, as I would not be surprised that they might, and remove the last two paragraphs-
